fields.v: Liu, Q., Zou, M., Zhang, H., Du, D., Xia, Y., Chen, H. (2026). Sharpen the Spec, Cut the Code: A Case for Generative File System with SYSSPEC. arXiv:2512.13047v4 [cs.OS], 10 Feb 2026
Conference — USENIX FAST (inferred: acknowledgements thank the FAST shepherd and the anonymous FAST reviewers); venue not printed; read from arXiv v4
fields.why: Acknowledgements thank a FAST shepherd and the anonymous FAST reviewers (p. 13), which implies acceptance at FAST, but no venue, year or proceedings are printed in the arXiv v4 text. Confirm the FAST '26 publication before keeping Conference.

fields.v: Institute of Parallel and Distributed Systems, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China (all authors)

Proposes an approach; secondary: Compares — SYSSPEC framework (formal-methods-inspired specification + LLM-based toolchain + DAG-structured spec patches), evaluated and compared with Normal/Oracle few-shot baselines on 4 LLMs, plus ablation, productivity study and performance of generated features; an Ext4 commit-history study (3,157 commits) serves as motivation

SYSSPEC (no version) with its toolchain agents SpecCompiler (CodeGen + SpecEval retry-with-feedback, two-phase generation), SpecValidator (SpecEval review + unit/regression tests), SpecAssistant (human-in-the-loop spec refinement with SpecFine); case system SPECFS (FUSE file system based on AtomFS). Artifact: github.com/LLMNativeOS/specfs-ae; llmnativeos.github.io/specfs

Multi-part specification in structured natural language with type annotations: Functionality spec (Hoare-style pre/post-conditions, invariants, system algorithm or intent; levels 1-3), Modularity spec (Rely-Guarantee interface contracts, modules <=500 LoC), Concurrency spec (locking pre/post-conditions, separate from functionality); DAG-structured spec patches (leaf, intermediate, root nodes) for evolution; generated C implementation

Developer writes spec (optionally refined by SpecAssistant) -> SpecCompiler per module: phase 1 sequential code, phase 2 concurrency instrumentation, each with CodeGen/SpecEval retry loop -> SpecValidator (spec review + xfstests/regression) -> compile and deploy (validated modules cached). Evolution: write spec patch -> regenerate from leaf to root nodes -> root replaces old module

Developer authors and validates the specification (SpecAssistant returns refined spec + C code for developer validation, or diagnostics on failure); debugging mostly at spec level; generation itself 'without any manual intervention'
Full workflow (spec -> generation -> validation -> evolution via spec patches) on SPECFS

Spec-as-source (authors: SPECFS 'specified entirely in specification'; 'Instead of manually modifying C implementation, developers add features by authoring a special patch... to the high-level specification'; toolchain regenerates the implementation)
New system generated from spec (AtomFS reimplementation, 45 modules) and evolution of the spec'd system (10 Ext4 features, 64 modules)
SPECFS: 45 modules, about 4,300 lines of generated C (ranks 42nd of 82 Linux 6.1.10 file systems by size); features: 64 functional modules; modules <=500 LoC, about 30K tokens per generation
Operating systems: concurrent in-memory FUSE file system in C (POSIX calls); Ext4 features (extent, inline data, delayed allocation, encryption, journaling, etc.); Linux dentry_lookup locking
Productivity study: two CS master's students and two PhD students; otherwise Not stated (authors)

Development time manual vs SYSSPEC (Extent 4.5 h vs 1.5 h; Rename 13 h vs 2.4 h); generation latency 'several minutes to tens of minutes'; about 30K tokens per module inference (design bound). No money or total tokens reported
Generation accuracy: module correct if it passes all AtomFS functional tests and is logically equivalent to manually written ground truth (manual inspection); xfstests pass/fail (754 cases)
Lines of code spec vs generated C (Fig. 12); comprehensibility of generated code (qualitative)
Development hours for two patches (4 students); spec LoC as effort proxy

Performance effects of generated features: storage reduction (inline data), non-contiguous I/O ratio (pre-allocation), block-pool accesses (rbtree), I/O operation counts (extent, delayed allocation); correctness of multi-granularity locking (dentry_lookup)

Automatic: functional tests and xfstests via SpecValidator; benchmarks (QEMU, Linux source, xv6 compilation, small/large file workloads). Manual: logical-equivalence inspection against ground-truth modules written by the authors; timing of students' development. Repetitions and statistics Not stated

Criterion: % of modules correct (passes AtomFS functional tests + manual logical equivalence with authors' ground truth). Agent = authors' SYSSPEC toolchain (no commercial agent). Values for GPT-5-minimal, Qwen3-32B and the Normal baseline only in Fig. 11 (not in text).
- SYSSPEC + SYSSPEC toolchain + Gemini-2.5-Pro: AtomFS 100% (45/45); features higher than baselines (Fig. 11b). Quality: works
- SYSSPEC + toolchain + DeepSeek-V3.1 Reasoning: AtomFS 100%; features higher than baselines. Quality: works
- SYSSPEC + toolchain + GPT-5-minimal: AtomFS value in Fig. 11a only (not stated in text); features higher than baselines (Fig. 11b). Quality: to read from figure
- SYSSPEC + toolchain + Qwen3-32B: AtomFS value in Fig. 11a only (not stated in text); features higher than baselines (Fig. 11b). Quality: to read from figure
- Oracle few-shot baseline (dependency APIs + ground-truth code) + Gemini-2.5-Pro: 81.8%. Baseline
- Oracle / Normal few-shot baselines + DS-V3.1, GPT-5-minimal, Qwen3-32B: values in Fig. 11 only. Baseline
- Ablation (DS-V3.1), concurrency-agnostic / thread-safe modules: Func only 40% (12/40) / 0% (0/5); +Mod 100% / 0%; +Con 100% / 80% (4/5); +SpecValidator 100% / 100% (5/5)
Other: SPECFS fails 64 of 754 xfstests, same as AtomFS (unimplemented functionality); up to 34.4% correctness improvement vs naive prompting on complex operations. Cost verdict: works (3.0x and 5.4x faster development than manual; latency minutes to tens of minutes)
fields.why: The r1 value still said SYSSPEC was 'higher than baselines' on AtomFS for GPT-5-minimal and Qwen3-32B, and gave a quality verdict for them; the text only states this for features (Fig. 11b, p. 11), and for AtomFS reports only Gemini/DS-V3.1 100% vs Oracle-Gemini 81.8%. Removed the unsupported claim; AtomFS values and verdicts for these two models must be read from Fig. 11a in the PDF (garbled in the text).

fields.v: Tasks: 45 AtomFS modules (40 concurrency-agnostic, 5 thread-safe) and 64 modules of 10 Ext4 features. Configurations: SYSSPEC vs Normal and Oracle few-shot baselines x 4 LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.1 Reasoning, GPT-5-minimal, Qwen3-32B); ablation on DS-V3.1; productivity manual vs SYSSPEC on 2 patches with 4 students. Held constant: same specification across models; same tests. Acceptance: AtomFS functional tests + manual equivalence; xfstests. Repetitions: Not stated. Human intervention: none during generation

AtomFS: SYSSPEC 100% on Gemini-2.5-Pro and DS-V3.1 vs 81.8% for the Oracle baseline with Gemini-2.5-Pro (other models in Fig. 11a only). Features: SYSSPEC higher than Normal and Oracle baselines on all four models (Fig. 11b, values not in text). Ablation: modularity spec needed for concurrency-agnostic modules (40% -> 100%), concurrency spec and SpecValidator for thread-safe modules (0% -> 80% -> 100%). Productivity 3.0x (Extent) and 5.4x (Rename). Spec LoC lower than C LoC for all layers/features. Significance: not tested
fields.why: r1 kept 'SYSSPEC higher than baselines on all four models for AtomFS', which the text does not state (only for features, p. 11). Restricted the all-models claim to features; AtomFS values for GPT-5-minimal and Qwen3-32B to be read from Fig. 11a.

fields.v: Distinguished SYSSPEC from baselines and ablation variants; repeatability: artefact with scripts provided, but single runs and no variance reported despite acknowledged LLM non-determinism. Limitations stated: FUSE user-space FS, no storage stack or crash consistency, no performance comparison with kernel file systems

SPECFS is user-space (FUSE), lacks storage stack and crash consistency; no apples-to-apples throughput comparison; future: apply to industrial file systems (EROFS, Ext4) starting from Ext2 baseline, bootstrap specs from documentation/source with SpecAssistant, decouple modules (Law of Demeter), integrate push-button formal verification. Upfront design effort higher (akin to Rust discipline)

Per-model accuracy for GPT-5-minimal, Qwen3-32B and Normal baselines only in Fig. 11 bar charts (not extractable from text); figure axes garbled in extraction. Artifact appendix: GitHub repo with gen.py/eval.py, needs Linux, FUSE, LLM API key (Gemini or DeepSeek). Ext4 study: 82.4% of commits bug fixes/maintenance, 5.1% features. Pre-registration: Not stated. Language: C (specs in structured natural language)

Yes (1): AtomFS modules, 10 features and xfstests described; artifact public
Partly (0.5): functional tests and xfstests, plus authors' manual equivalence check against their own ground truth
fields.why: Correctness needs both the AtomFS functional tests / xfstests (independent) and a manual equivalence check against ground truth the authors wrote themselves (p. 11). Yes is arguable if tests are taken as the criterion; Partly kept because the authors' manual judgement is part of it.

fields.v: Partly (0.5): accuracy, development time and LoC defined; token/money cost not measured
fields.why: Quality metrics are defined; cost appears only as human development time on 2 patches (p. 12) and an informal latency ('several minutes to tens of minutes'); no tokens or money. Time is a cost metric under §6, so Yes is arguable; Partly kept because LLM cost is not measured.

fields.v: Yes (1): Normal and Oracle few-shot baselines on the same models; ablation
No (0): no repetitions or statistical analysis reported
Partly (0.5): accuracy claims supported; productivity claim rests on 2 tasks and 4 students; 'highly effective' generalisation beyond one FS
fields.why: Judgement: accuracy and ablation claims follow from the results, but productivity (3.0x/5.4x) rests on 2 tasks and 4 students with no repetitions, and 'highly effective' (abstract) generalises from one user-space FS. Partly is a reasonable reading.
